concepts.name: Negotiation as joint decision
concepts.summary: Explain that negotiation is two parties seeking agreement on price or terms where each can say no, and that both must accept the result.

concepts.name: Interests versus positions
concepts.summary: Distinguish what a party asks for (position) from the underlying reason or need (interest) it serves.

concepts.name: BATNA
aliases: best alternative to a negotiated agreement
concepts.summary: Define a BATNA as your best option if no deal is reached and explain why it sets your real bargaining strength.

concepts.name: Reservation point
concepts.summary: Recall that the reservation point is the worst deal you would still accept, beyond which you prefer your alternative.

concepts.name: Target and aspiration
concepts.summary: Understand that a target is the ambitious but realistic outcome you aim for, set above your reservation point.

concepts.name: Offer and counteroffer
concepts.summary: Recognise the basic move sequence in which one side proposes terms and the other accepts, rejects or answers with a different proposal.

concepts.name: Preparation before talking
concepts.summary: Explain why researching market values, the other side and your own priorities before the meeting improves outcomes.

misconceptions.text: Negotiation is a fight in which one side's gain is exactly the other side's loss.
Your reservation point is the same as your target.
You can negotiate well without any preparation if you are confident and quick.

concepts.name: Setting a reservation point from BATNA
concepts.summary: Calculate a reservation point by valuing your BATNA and adjusting for costs, risks and non-price factors.

concepts.name: Zone of possible agreement
concepts.summary: Identify the overlap between both sides' reservation points, and recognise that no overlap means no deal is possible.

concepts.name: Anchoring
concepts.summary: Apply the effect that an early number pulls the final outcome toward it, by making a well-justified first offer.

concepts.name: Making concessions
concepts.summary: Make concessions that are gradual, reciprocal and shrinking in size so they signal limits without giving away value.

concepts.name: Multiple issues in a deal
concepts.summary: Recognise that deals include price plus terms such as timing, scope, benefits and risk that can all be negotiated.

concepts.name: Justifying with objective criteria
concepts.summary: Support a request with external standards such as market data or precedent rather than preference alone.

concepts.name: Active listening and questions
concepts.summary: Use open questions and paraphrasing to uncover the other side's priorities and constraints.

misconceptions.text: Whoever makes the first offer always loses because they reveal too much.
Agreement is possible whenever both sides keep talking long enough.
Large early concessions build goodwill and are returned automatically.

concepts.name: Estimating the other side's BATNA
concepts.summary: Infer the counterpart's alternatives and likely reservation point from market evidence and their behaviour to judge the ZOPA.

concepts.name: Trading issues through logrolling
concepts.summary: Analyse differing priorities across issues and trade what you value less for what you value more to create joint gain.

concepts.name: Multiple equivalent simultaneous offers
concepts.summary: Present several packages of equal value to you to learn which the counterpart prefers.

concepts.name: Responding to anchors
concepts.summary: Assess an extreme first offer and respond by rejecting its basis, re-anchoring with data or refocusing on criteria.

concepts.name: Concession pattern analysis
concepts.summary: Interpret the size and timing of the counterpart's concessions to estimate how close they are to their limit.

concepts.name: Separating people from the problem
concepts.summary: Handle emotion and relationship concerns separately from the substantive issues so they do not distort the terms.

concepts.name: Closing and documenting agreement
concepts.summary: Summarise agreed terms, test for unresolved points, and put them in writing so both parties can sign.

misconceptions.text: Trading issues means splitting every difference down the middle.
Ignoring an extreme anchor is enough to neutralise its influence.
A verbal handshake means the deal is closed and details can be sorted out later.

concepts.name: Evaluating package value
concepts.summary: Judge competing packages by weighting issues with a scoring model that includes risk and time value, not price alone.

concepts.name: Improving BATNA and reframing leverage
concepts.summary: Evaluate ways to strengthen your alternatives or weaken the counterpart's, and choose the one worth the cost.

concepts.name: Contingent and risk-sharing terms
concepts.summary: Analyse when differing beliefs about the future can be bridged by terms such as bonuses, earn-outs or price adjustments.

concepts.name: Deadlock diagnosis
concepts.summary: Diagnose whether a stalemate stems from no ZOPA, hidden interests, face-saving or process, and select a remedy.

concepts.name: Negotiating with multiple parties
concepts.summary: Analyse hidden decision makers, agents and coalitions and adapt the approach to each.

concepts.name: Hardball tactics and responses
concepts.summary: Judge tactics such as deadlines, good cop/bad cop and nibbling, and decide whether to name, ignore or counter them.

concepts.name: Ethics and trust in bargaining
concepts.summary: Evaluate the line between acceptable withholding or puffery and deception, and its effect on reputation and enforceability.

misconceptions.text: Lying about your reservation point is a normal and harmless part of negotiating.
Every tactic from a counterpart should be met with matching toughness.
An impasse always means the other side is being unreasonable.

concepts.name: Designing negotiation strategy
concepts.summary: Design a negotiation plan across sequence, venue, coalition and timing that fits the power balance and the relationship horizon.

concepts.name: Creating new value structures
concepts.summary: Invent deal structures such as bundled long-term contracts or option rights that open gains neither side initially saw.

concepts.name: Judging fairness and sustainability of deals
concepts.summary: Evaluate whether a deal will hold by assessing perceived fairness, enforcement and incentives to renege.

concepts.name: Adapting across cultures and contexts
concepts.summary: Assess how culture, hierarchy and communication norms alter the meaning of offers, silence and concessions, and adjust.

concepts.name: Behavioural bias management
concepts.summary: Evaluate and counter biases such as overconfidence, fixed-pie thinking and escalation of commitment in yourself and others.

concepts.name: Mediating and coaching negotiations
concepts.summary: Create a process in which a third party or team negotiates well, including mandates, authority limits and debriefs.

concepts.name: Portfolio and repeated-game negotiation
concepts.summary: Evaluate how a deal sets precedent and shapes future bargaining, and trade single-deal gains against long-term position.

misconceptions.text: Expert negotiators succeed mainly through charisma and instinct rather than structured preparation.
The same tactics work equally well in every culture and context.
Maximising the result of each single deal is always the best long-term strategy.
